'''''Geranium lucidum''''', commonly known as '''shining cranesbill'''<ref>Hackney, P. (Ed) 1992. ''Stewart and Corry's Flora of the North-east of Ireland''. Institute of Irish Studies, The Queen's University of Belfast {{ISBN|0-85389-446-9}}</ref> or (in North America) '''shining geranium''' or '''shiny geranium''', is a herbaceous annual plant of the genus ''[[Geranium]]''. It is native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa. It has been introduced to North America as a garden plant and in places, particularly the [[Pacific Northwest]], has become naturalised and is viewed as an [[invasive species]] and [[noxious weed]].

==Description==
The shining cranesbill is an annual plant with stems up to {{convert|35|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long, brittle, fleshy, hairless and often red. Leaves round or kidney-shaped and glossy, palmately-lobed or divided bluntly to about two-thirds of their depth, sometimes with short hairs on the upper surface. Flowers  with parts in fives, with sharply keeled [[sepal]]s and bright pink, rounded petals, some {{convert|10|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} in diameter, the {{convert|8|to|10|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} petals having long bases and flat blades. These are borne in pairs from May to August. The fruits are beaked capsules, ridged and slightly hairy, at least on the edges, and splitting open into five parts. The seeds are smooth. The whole plant has a tendency to turn red.<ref name=Keble>[[Martin, W. Keble]] 1965. ''The Concise British Flora in Colour''  Ebury Press and Michael Joseph</ref><ref>Parnell, J. and Curtis. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora.'' Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-1-85918-478-3}}</ref><ref name=Harrap>{{cite book|author=Harrap, Simon|title=Harrap's Wild Flowers|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rwRpBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA104 |year=2014 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=978-1-4081-8987-0 |page=104}}</ref>

==Distribution==
[[File:Geranium lucidum, Wales.jpg|thumb|Shining cranesbill on a wall in Wales]]
The shining cranesbill is native to Europe, Asia as far east as the Himalayas and northern Africa.<ref name=PFAF>{{cite web |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Geranium+lucidum |title=''Geranium lucidum'' – L. |publisher=Plants for a Future |accessdate=28 June 2016}}</ref> This plant is common in [[Great Britain]] and [[Ireland]],<ref>Clapham, A.R.; Tutin, T.G.; Warburg, E.F. 1968. ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles (Second Edition)'' Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-04656-4}}</ref> especially in the southwest and west, but uncommon in Scotland. It is found at altitudes of up to {{convert|610|m|ft|-1|abbr=on}}.<ref name=Harrap/> It has been grown as a garden plant in parts of the United States and has become naturalised in the Pacific Northwest.<ref name=PFAF/>

==Habitat==
The shining cranesbill is common on limestone rocks and walls, and in churchyards on roadside verges, banks, gardens and bare ground; it thrives on chalky or sandy soil.<ref name=Harrap/> It is also common on acid soils and shady banks.<ref name=Keble/> The plant has good dispersal abilities because the seed is explosively thrown out of the capsule, allowing the plant to move up slopes and exploit crevices in tree trunks and recesses in walls that are higher than the parent plant.<ref name=KingCounty/>

==Invasive species==
In parts of the United States including [[California]], [[Washington (state)|Washington state]] and the [[Willamette Valley]] in Oregon, shining cranesbill has become naturalised. It was first detected in the US in 1971 and has since been declared a [[noxious weed]] in Washington and Oregon.<ref name=USDA/> A 2013 survey by USDA reported that it was present in five counties in Washington, thirteen in Oregon and two in California. It was detected in Canada in 1982, on [[Vancouver Island]] in [[British Columbia]], and has been introduced into Australia and New Zealand.<ref name=USDA>{{cite web |url=https://www.aphis.usda.gov/plant_health/plant_pest_info/weeds/downloads/wra/Geranium_lucidum_WRA.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150213053035/http://www.aphis.usda.gov/plant_health/plant_pest_info/weeds/downloads/wra/Geranium_lucidum_WRA.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 13, 2015 |title=Weed Risk Assessment for ''Geranium lucidum'' L. (Geraniaceae) – Shining cranesbill |author=Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service |date=11 June 2013 |publisher=USDA }}</ref>

When naturalised in the Pacific Northwest, it is often seen in association with the related European plant, [[Geranium robertianum|herb Robert]] (''Geranium robertianum''), also classified as a noxious weed. In these areas, shining cranesbill seems to thrive in woodlands and forest glades, where it tends to overwhelm the native plants. State legislation has been enacted making it "prohibited to transport, buy, sell, offer for sale, or to distribute plants or plant parts, seeds in packets, blends or "wildflower mixes" of this species, into or within the state of Washington".<ref name=KingCounty>{{cite web |url=http://www.kingcounty.gov/environment/animals-and-plants/noxious-weeds/weed-identification/shiny-geranium.aspx |title=Shiny geranium |work=Noxious Weeds |publisher=King County, Washington |accessdate=28 June 2016}}</ref>
